analysis.one_liner: Bans Medicare payments to hospitals and nursing homes owned by private equity or real estate trusts.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would cut Medicare payments to hospitals and nursing homes owned by private equity firms or real estate trusts after a 3-year phase-out, has been referred to two House committees and has 12 Democratic cosponsors with no committee vote or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make hospitals and skilled nursing facilities that are owned or controlled by private equity funds or real estate investment trusts (REITs) ineligible for Medicare payments, giving currently PE- or REIT-owned facilities three years to find new owners before the cutoff takes effect [S2]. The goal is to remove private equity control from hospital and nursing home care for the roughly 65 million Americans on Medicare. The bill was introduced in March 2026 and referred to the House Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees, where it has had no action since.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare patients who get care at hospitals and nursing homes owned by private equity funds or REITs, if the loss of Medicare revenue pushes those facilities to sell to non-PE operators or be restructured under different ownership. Research on private equity in health care links the model to higher prices, staff cuts, and facility closures, so removing the ownership model aims to protect care quality and access. Taxpayers also benefit indirectly if fewer Medicare dollars flow out of the hospital system as returns to investment firms.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare patients at private equity-owned facilities

how_it_helps.text: Adds a new prohibition to Medicare law so that no Medicare payment may go to any hospital or skilled nursing facility owned or controlled by a private equity fund, a corporation a PE fund controls, or a REIT [S2].

Applies the ownership test broadly: an entity controls a hospital if it holds 10% or more of its voting securities or directs its management or policies, including through affiliates, which limits the ability to evade the ban through shell structures [S2].

Makes a covered firm jointly and severally liable for penalties its facilities incur for violating the ban, so the parent fund cannot escape accountability behind the local facility's corporate veil [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Private equity funds and REITs that own or control hospitals and skilled nursing facilities would lose Medicare revenue, the main payment source for most such facilities, forcing them to sell or restructure within three years of enactment [S2]. If a facility cannot find a non-PE, non-REIT buyer in that window, its Medicare patients could lose access to care at that facility, and the facility's workers could face job changes or losses under new ownership.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity funds and healthcare REITs

drawbacks.text: The three-year phase-out is a hard deadline: any PE- or REIT-owned facility that cannot find a new buyer or restructure in time would simply lose all Medicare revenue, and its Medicare patients would have to find care elsewhere, which is a real access risk in areas where the facility is the main provider [S2].

The bill targets ownership, not conduct: it would bar Medicare payments to a well-run PE- or REIT-owned facility just as surely as to a badly run one, and it leaves untouched any quality problems at facilities owned by other corporations or chains.

The definition of a covered firm is built on exemptions in the Investment Company Act of 1940 and a 10% voting-control test, so the lines can be gamed in either direction and the Secretary would be left to make case-by-case control determinations [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit for Medicare patients is large, because private equity ownership of hospitals and nursing homes has been repeatedly linked to worse staffing, higher costs, and closures, and this bill would remove that ownership model from Medicare entirely rather than just regulate it. But the costs are real and fall partly on the same patients the bill tries to protect: the three-year deadline gives facilities little room to find new owners, and a facility that fails would cut off Medicare-covered care for its own patients. The bill would have been stronger with a transition plan or a conduct-based trigger alongside the ownership ban. As introduced, it is a blunt but well-aimed instrument whose outcome would depend heavily on how facilities restructure.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to two House committees, which have not taken it up, so it is waiting and may simply run out of time.

narrative.text: Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon introduced the bill on March 12, 2026, joined by six Democratic colleagues as original cosponsors, and it was referred to both the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees [S1][S2][S4].
Since the referral, the action history shows no hearings, no markups, no committee votes, and no floor action [S4].
Twelve House Democrats have cosponsored the bill; no Republican has [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, private equity funds and REITs that own hospitals and nursing homes, because with no committee action the bill poses no near-term threat to their Medicare revenue or their ownership of health care facilities.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity funds and healthcare REITs

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred; all 13 supporters are Democrats (the sponsor plus 12 cosponsors out of 217 House Democrats) and no Republican has signed on, but the absence of a roll call means the partisan split is not yet tested.

industries.industry: Private equity funds with hospital and nursing home investments
industries.note: The bill would cut off Medicare payments, the core revenue of hospitals and nursing homes, to any facility a PE fund owns or controls, with a three-year exit window [S2]. This directly targets the PE model of buying health care facilities, restructuring them, and extracting returns, which studies have linked to staffing cuts, higher prices, and closures that hit Medicare patients and their families.

industries.industry: Real estate investment trusts that own hospital and nursing home property
industries.note: REITs that own or control hospital and skilled nursing real estate would be treated the same as PE firms, and facilities under their control would lose Medicare payments after the phase-out [S2]. REIT ownership is often the financing layer behind PE-style health care deals, so the bill closes that route as well.

industries.industry: Non-PE hospital operators and health systems
industries.note: Facilities owned by hospitals, health systems, nonprofits, or other operators outside the covered definitions would face no new restriction, and any patient or asset flow away from PE- and REIT-owned facilities would go to them. They could also acquire PE-owned facilities as owners are forced to sell within three years [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With no action in committee since referral, 12 cosponsors out of 217 House Democrats, no Republican support, and jurisdiction split between two committees, the bill is unlikely to get a committee vote, much less floor time, before the 119th Congress ends in January 2027. Bills at this stage — recently introduced, referred to multiple committees, no bipartisan sponsorship — overwhelmingly die when the Congress adjourns and must be reintroduced from scratch.
